### `crimewidthkill` (HIGH) -- filed 2026-09-10 -- CLOSED by `#529` (its chain closed 2026-09-26; committed 2026-10-02)

**CLOSED by `#529`**: the width is DECLINED -- member 3, one latched `(once)` announce and a goto to the common tail -- after FAULT (member 5) was weighed and rejected on pass 1 (`crimewidthkill/fable_pass1_20260913.md`: FAULT's only host trace is a `debug()` silent when free-running; a decline keeps the guest running; no CRIME document establishes a bus error).  Rung-3 witness committed 3/15, fix 15/15; detector `regress/crime_width_probe.py`, 226 rows, gate 14.  The text below is the 2026-09-10 filing.

`dev_sgi_ip32.c`, `DEVICE_ACCESS(crime)`, grep anchor `fatal("crime access len = %i!\n", len);`: the
handler is a bare `if (len == 8) {...} else if (len == 4) {...} else { fatal(...); exit(1); }`. There is
no other width arm, so **every other access length -- 1, 2, and anything wider -- ends the emulator.** A
byte load is an ordinary thing for a guest or a PROM to do while probing, and nothing about the device's
mapping advertises a width restriction.

`machine_sgi.c` installs it with `dev_crime_init(machine, mem, 0x14000000, ...)` on the IP32 machines.
CRIME is the memory and interrupt controller: one of the first things any IP32 guest touches.

**The disposition is the interesting part, because member 5 (FAULT) is genuinely available here, which it
usually is not.** `memory_rw.c` converts a failed device callback into an architectural access exception
for **MIPS and M88K only** -- and this device is on MIPS. So `return 0` is not a silent decline: it is a
positive statement that the access could not be serviced, delivered as the bus error real hardware gives.
That is the `dev_unreadable.c` idiom, and `machine_sgi.c` already installs `dev_unreadable` ten times for
exactly this reason -- the PROM and NetBSD probe absent regions and RELY on the failure. A round here
should weigh FAULT against DECLINE rather than defaulting to decline as most of this queue does. Not
measured, no witness; the rung-3 attempt is owed and looks cheap.

### `vmedefaultkill` (HIGH) -- filed 2026-09-10

`dev_vme.c`, default arm: it announces with **`debug()`** and then calls `exit(1)`.

*** THIS ONE IS WORSE THAN THE USUAL SHAPE, AND THE REASON IS THE DIAGNOSTIC LEVEL. *** Every other
unimplemented-register kill in this queue announces with `fatal()`, which this fork has measured cannot be
silenced by `-q` -- `fatal()` has no early-out and goes straight to `va_debug`. This one uses `debug()`,
which does have one (`if ((quiet_mode && !ss) || v < 0) return;`), so at default verbosity **the message
is not printed at all and the emulator dies with no output explaining why.** A user sees the process
vanish; a gate sees a non-zero exit and no diagnostic to grep. That makes it the hardest member of the
class to DIAGNOSE, independent of how hard it is to trigger.

`machine_mvme88k.c` installs it unconditionally (`vme addr=...`, `VME2_BASE`) on a machine this project
actively boots -- the same constructor attaches the PCC2 the recent rounds are about. Probing a bus
controller's register space is exactly what firmware does.

Disposition: member 5 (FAULT) is **available** -- M88K is one of the two families `memory_rw.c` delivers a
failed-device exception for -- so `return 0` gives the guest the bus error real VME hardware would. Member
3 is the alternative and would need the announce **promoted from `debug()` to `fatal()`** to be worth
anything, which is a second change the round must make deliberately rather than inherit.

### `fbctrlportkill` (HIGH) -- filed 2026-09-10

`dev_fbctrl.c`: **the PORT arm accepts an out-of-range port number with a warning and STORES it, and the
DATA arm then calls `exit(1)` on that same stored value.** A two-step, guest-driven host kill in which the
first step looks handled:

```c
case DEV_FBCTRL_PORT:  d->current_port = idata;                 /* stored FIRST */
                       if (idata >= DEV_FBCTRL_NPORTS)
                               fatal("[ WARNING: ... out of range! ]\n");   /* warned SECOND */
case DEV_FBCTRL_DATA:  if (d->current_port < 0 || d->current_port >= DEV_FBCTRL_NPORTS) {
                               fatal(...); exit(1); }
```

A reader auditing the PORT arm sees a range check and a diagnostic and concludes the case is handled. The
check does nothing but print.

*** AND THE TWO GUARDS TEST DIFFERENT QUANTITIES, which is the guard-field/body-field discriminator the
pre-table check mandates. *** PORT tests `idata`, a `uint64_t`; DATA tests `d->current_port`, an `int`
(verified in the struct). The store between them **truncates**. Both halves of the DATA guard are live:
writing `0xffffffff` warns at PORT and lands `current_port == -1`, killing via the `< 0` half; writing
`0x100000000` warns at PORT and truncates to a perfectly valid `0`, so the warning fires about a value
that turns out fine. **The warning and the kill are keyed to different numbers**, so neither predicts the
other, and a detector must not assume the warning marks the killing set.

**The fix's first question is ORDER:** refusing the store in the PORT arm closes the DATA kill without
touching the DATA arm at all -- one line moved, and it makes the DATA guard the belt-and-braces it reads
as. Declining at DATA instead leaves the model holding a selector it has agreed to and cannot use.

Reachability: `machine_test.c` attaches fbctrl at TWO sites, so it is on `testmips` and `testarm` --
**the machines this project's own gates drive**. Third and fourth kills in the same file, recorded so a
round does not close on one: `fbctrl_command()` has `default: fatal(...); exit(1)`, reached by writing a
command byte to the COMMAND port, and the `DEVICE_ACCESS` default arm is another.

*All three came from the GPT-6 Astra exit audit's six E1 predicates
(`regress/artifacts/queuetriage/codex_exitaudit_20260910.txt`). Every element above was re-derived locally
by opening the files.*

### `ppcrldiclzero` (HIGH) -- filed 2026-09-10 -- *** FIXED AND SHIPPED AS `#522`; see the CHANGELOG round block. The reading below stands and was CONFIRMED at rung 3 before the edit (19/27 -> 24/27, 190 of 190 census cells wrong pre-fix and none after). ***

`cpu_ppc_instr.c`, grep anchor `X(rldicl)`: **the handler always writes ZERO to its destination
register, for every operand, every rotate amount and every mask begin.**

```c
uint64_t tmp = cpu->cd.ppc.gpr[rs], tmp2;
while (sh-- != 0) { ... rotate tmp left by one ... }
tmp2 = 0;
while (mb <= 63) {
        tmp |= ((uint64_t)1 << (63-mb));      /*  the MASK goes into tmp  */
        mb ++;
}
cpu->cd.ppc.gpr[ra] = tmp & tmp2;             /*  tmp2 is STILL 0  */
```

`tmp2` is assigned `0` and never assigned again. The `|=` also corrupts the rotated value it lands in,
but that is moot: the result is ANDed with zero either way.

**The sibling two functions down shows the intended shape, which makes the diagnosis certain rather than
inferred.** `X(rldicr)` does the same rotate and then CLEARS bits in `tmp` (`tmp &= ~((uint64_t)1 <<
(63-me))`), assigning `tmp` directly. `X(rldicl)` was written the other way round -- build a mask, then
AND -- and the mask was accumulated into the wrong variable. **The fix is one character:** `tmp |=`
becomes `tmp2 |=`.

*** Why this is the most serious thing in today's batch. *** `rldicl` is not an obscure corner: it is
**the** canonical 64-bit PowerPC masking and zero-extension instruction, emitted constantly by compilers
(`rldicl rA,rS,0,32` is the standard 32-bit zero-extend). Every other defect filed today needs a guest to
touch a particular register, width or offset. This one is wrong on the ordinary path, for ordinary code,
on every execution.

Reachability is wired and checked: `case PPC_30_RLDICL: ic->f = instr(rldicl); break;` in the primary
decoder, reached whenever `cpu->cd.ppc.bits == 64`; the 32-bit path deliberately goes to `bad`. So it is
live on every 64-bit PowerPC CPU model in this tree and dead on the 32-bit ones. **No regression file in
the tree mentions `rldicl`** (`grep -rn rldicl regress/` outside artifacts returns nothing), which is how
an always-zero result survived.

**It is NOT a shift defect, which matters for scoping.** The census that found it explicitly records the
computed counts here as SAFE (mask counts 0..63, rotate counts 1..31, hazard form NONE). It is a plain
variable mix-up found while looking at something else, and it belongs to neither `shiftubcensus` nor
`mipsextshift` but to its own correctness round.

Not measured, no witness. The rung-3 attempt is owed first and looks unusually cheap: any 64-bit PowerPC
machine, one `rldicl` with a nonzero source, and a register readback -- the wanted value is anything but
zero and the pre-fix build must show zero. **A guest-visible wrong RESULT is a far easier oracle than the
process-death oracles most of this queue needs.** Check first whether the existing PowerPC gates already
execute one and pass anyway, because a green gate over an always-zero instruction would itself be a
finding about the gates.

*Found by the GPT-6 Astra seat under the found-something-else licence while answering a tree-wide
shift-UB census (`regress/artifacts/shiftcensus/codex_census_20260910.txt`). Verified locally by opening
the handler before filing.*

### `ppcrldimimask` (HIGH) -- filed 2026-09-10

`cpu_ppc_instr.c`, grep anchor `X(rldimi)`: the rotate loop's post-decrement **always** leaves its shift
variable at -1, so the insert mask always runs to bit 63 instead of `63 - SH`. **The instruction
overwrites the `64 - SH` destination bits the architecture requires it to PRESERVE**, for every `SH != 0`.

Measured, destination seeded to 0 and an all-ones source: `SH=8` gives all-ones where the architecture
wants the low byte preserved; `SH=32` gives all-ones where it wants the low word preserved; `SH=0` agrees,
and is the one safe case. This is the standard bitfield **insert** -- a compiler using it to splice a field
destroys everything to the right of that field.

*** The durable repair is NOT to patch the `63 - sh` expression. *** That loop idiom is shared by
`rldicl`, `rldicr` and `rldimi`; `rldicr` survives only because it never reads the variable again. **Any
future edit that reaches for it after the rotate loop in any of the three will be wrong the same way.**
Save it before the loop instead. Same reachability and the same gate blind spot as `ppcrldiclzero`.

### `ppcrlwimiwidth` (HIGH) -- filed 2026-09-10

`cpu_ppc_instr.c`, grep anchor `X(rlwimi)`: the 32-bit rotate is performed at **64-bit width** in the
64-bit build, so high-half source data leaks into the low 32 bits. The file is compiled twice and the
operand type is 64 bits in one of them; the architecture specifies a 32-bit rotate over the source's LOW
half only, and **the high half plays no part whatsoever**.

Measured with source `0xAAAAAAAA0000000F`, destination seeded, shift 4: `got 0x5a5a5a5aaaaaaaf0` against
`want 0x5a5a5a5a000000f0`. The `0xAAAAAA` is high-half data that cannot architecturally reach there.

**Attribution is pinned by two companion rows.** `rlwinm` on the same source and shift is correct, because
it casts to 32 bits before rotating, and `rlwimi` at shift 0 is correct because the ternary short-circuits
the rotate. So the defect is the missing truncation in this one handler, not the shape of the expression.

*A row testing this is vacuous unless the source's two halves DIFFER: the measuring seat's own first draft
used an all-ones source, under which a 64-bit rotate and a true 32-bit one agree bit for bit, and it
corrected the row rather than shipping it green.*

**Adjacent, not a defect but recorded so a round does not rediscover it:** `rldic`, `rldcl` and `rldcr` are
not implemented at all -- the decoder's default swallows them. `rldic` in particular is documented and
compiler-emitted.

### `ppcrldiclzero` -- *** WITNESSED AT RUNG 3 2026-09-10, AND IT IS A CLASS. ***

Confirmed on three unmodified in-tree machines including the Power Mac G5 model: **190 of 190 census
cells return zero** on the committed build and 0 of 190 under the one-character repair (19/27 -> 24/27,
logs `witness_committed.out` / `witness_fix.out`).

**Three ways the original filing understated it.** (a) **Two tokens are wrong, not one**, and the obvious
repair -- deleting the AND -- was BUILT AND MEASURED STILL WRONG on 126 of 190 cells; it ships an OR where
the architecture says AND, and is worse in one specific way because it removes the always-zero signature
while leaving the value wrong. (b) **A second channel: it corrupts CONTROL FLOW.** The record form reports
equal-to-zero on every execution, so any branch on a masked compare takes the wrong arm. (c) It is
reachable on a real machine model, not only synthetic ones.

**The gate finding is structural and stronger than "no gate covers it":** both PowerPC gates drive a
32-bit processor, and the decoder sends the whole 64-bit instruction group to its bad path in 32-bit mode.
**No gate has ever instantiated a 64-bit PowerPC CPU at all** -- *** FALSE, AND CORRECTED AT THE END OF THIS FILE (search `MY GATE CLAIM WAS FALSE'): a gate DOES construct them; what no gate does is CHECK THEIR INSTRUCTION RESULTS. The sentence is kept because it is what two commit messages say. *** -- so that group is invisible by construction
rather than by omission -- one coverage hole with one cause, closed by a single 64-bit probe. Severity
ceiling stated honestly: nothing in-tree BOOTS a 64-bit PowerPC guest, which is why the witness is rung 3.

### `mipsextshift` -- *** THE DESIGN REVIEW'S FOUR CORRECTIONS, 2026-09-10 ***

**(1) Plain `dext` has NO bad field pairs, so the entry's own title was wrong.** Enumerated per opcode
across all 1024 raw pairs: EXT has 496 negative counts, **DEXT has zero**, and DEXTM and DEXTU have 496
each. The two variants add 32 to the field they widen **before packing the arguments for the shared
handler**, so `X(dext)` is fed out-of-range fields rather than generating them. *A fix aimed at `dext`
would have been aimed at the wrong place.*

**(2) There ARE admission gates**, contrary to this entry's broader claim. SPECIAL3 rejects older
ISA/revision combinations, R5900 takes another path, and a `$zero` destination selects a NOP. The field
domains are unconstrained *when the handler actually runs*, but not every model or destination reaches it.

**(3) A Reserved Instruction exception is PERMITTED, not MANDATED** -- which is exactly the overclaim this
entry warned itself against. The manuals make the excessive field sum UNPREDICTABLE, and the manual's own
definition of that term permits arbitrary exceptions while forbidding processor halt or hang. Declining is
a sound policy; claiming the architecture requires RI would overstate the evidence.

**(4) The `dins`-family execution handlers do not exist in this tree**, so the sibling question is partly
moot.

**The prescribed fix is two DECODER guards, not a mask and not a cast:** reject `lsb + msbd + 1 > 32` for
EXT and `> 64` for the shared DEXT/DEXTM/DEXTU case **after** the variant adjustments, and do it **before
the `$zero` NOP shortcut** -- the ordering matters, because a NOP taken first would swallow the rejection.
That places the bound where the fields are normalised, which is the only point at which one bound serves
all three variants.

### `ppcrldiclzero` / `ppcrldimimask` / `ppcrlwimiwidth` -- *** MY GATE CLAIM WAS FALSE. Corrected 2026-09-10. ***

I wrote, into three rows, a queue entry and two commit messages, that **"no gate in this tree instantiates
a 64-bit PowerPC CPU at all, so the whole 64-bit-only instruction group is invisible BY CONSTRUCTION."**
**The first half is false.** Gate 9 enumerates every advertised machine type and subtype, including three
that default to the PPC970, so 64-bit PowerPC CPUs are constructed by a gate today and always have been.

**The correct and narrower finding is that NO GATE CHECKS THEIR INSTRUCTION RESULTS.** Gate 9 is a
construction check with no PowerPC result oracle, and both PowerPC gates drive a 32-bit part, selected
*explicitly* in their probes rather than inherited by default. The defects were invisible because nothing
executes these instructions and inspects the answer — not because nothing builds the processor.

*** That distinction is this project's own witness ladder one level up, and I walked straight past it. ***
The ladder's rung-2 clause says in as many words that machine construction proves presence and **not**
reachability, and is a reproduction only for defects construction itself executes. I applied that rule
carefully to witnesses all day and then made exactly the error it warns about while reasoning about gates.
A gate that constructs a CPU is a rung-2 gate; these defects need a rung-3 one.

**The closure is smaller than my framing implied:** wire the existing 19-row probe into the PowerPC gate,
asserting its score *and* its completion sentinel. That closes the missing instruction-result check. It
does **not** close all 64-bit PowerPC coverage, and the review says so explicitly rather than letting the
round claim it does.


### `mipsextshift` -- DESIGNED 2026-09-10, and the design CONFIRMED the placement already prescribed here while correcting two of my premises

The entry above prescribes two decoder guards placed after the variant adjustments and before the
`$zero` NOP shortcut. **A design review (`regress/artifacts/mipsextshift/codex_guards_RETRY_20260910.txt`,
GPT-6 Astra at max, zero content flags) confirms that placement and supplies the proof the entry did not
have** -- the shared predicate moved BEFORE the adjustments has a left-hand side of at most 63, so it is
never `> 64` and **rejects nothing whatever**: a guard that reads correctly, compiles, and is identically
inert. That is the ordering mutant the detector owes.

    EXT block:                if (lsb + msbd + 1 > 32) { ic->f = instr(reserved); break; }
    DEXT/DEXTM/DEXTU block:   if (lsb + msbd + 1 > 64) { ic->f = instr(reserved); break; }

The inner `break` leaves `switch (s6)`, which is what keeps the later `rt == MIPS_GPR_ZERO` rewrite from
overwriting the refusal -- so an invalid pair targeting register zero still takes the exception. That is
deliberate rather than incidental.

**TWO PREMISES OF MINE WERE WRONG.** I gave plain `DEXT` the constraint `pos + size <= 32`; the
specification says **63**, because `DEXT` may extract a field crossing bit 31. The conclusion that `DEXT`
is safe survives; the reason I gave for it did not. And I wrote that a negative shift count is "in
practice reduced modulo the width" -- **C99 guarantees no such thing**, and the two handlers do not even
fail alike: `X(ext)` uses the negative `int` directly, while `X(dext)` converts it to `uint64_t` first,
giving an enormous unsigned count. Two routes to undefined behaviour, one of which my description did not
contain.

The 496 figure is confirmed three times over, and more cleanly than I derived it: all three expressions
reduce to `31 - (b + m)`, negative exactly when `b + m >= 32`.

**DISPOSITION: raise the architectural Reserved Instruction exception** (`ic->f = instr(reserved);`), on
this file's own precedent -- the ISA-support check immediately above the switch already does exactly that.
`X(reserved)` syncs the pc and calls `mips_cpu_exception(..., EXCEPTION_RI, ...)`; it does **not** call
`exit()`. The specification permits the choice: *"UNPREDICTABLE operations may cause arbitrary
exceptions."*

*** THE BLOCKER IS REACHABILITY, NOT DESIGN. *** `EXT` is MIPS32 Release 2 and the doubleword forms are
MIPS64 Release 2, so they are not available merely because this tree boots a MIPS machine, and **no
machine has been named that runs them.** The rung-3 attempt is owed before this may be recorded
documented-only. **Scope is TWO changes, not three** -- `DEXTM`/`DEXTU`/`DEXT` share a site, a predicate
and a handler; `EXT` is the second -- and they combine into one only if a single parameterised
decoder-selection test covers all four opcodes.

### `mipsextsignext` (LOW) -- filed 2026-09-10

`X(ext)` reads `uint32_t rs = reg(ic->arg[1]);`, truncating to 32 bits and asking nothing about the upper
half. **MIPS64 Volume II requires `EXT`'s source to be a properly sign-extended 32-bit value**, so a
64-bit register holding a value that is not a sign-extension of its low word is accepted and extracted
from silently.

Found by the `mipsextshift` design review while answering a different question, which said so plainly:
*"The proposed range checks do not address that separate condition."*

**Filed separately rather than folded in**, because the fix shape differs: `mipsextshift`'s guards are a
decode-time predicate over two instruction fields, decidable when the instruction is translated, while
this is a **run-time property of a register value** and cannot be checked in the decoder at all. Same
instruction, different mechanism.

**LOW, and the reason matters:** like the range case this is UNPREDICTABLE-on-violation, but unlike it
there is **no undefined behaviour in the host** -- the truncation is well-defined C. The cost is a wrong
guest answer in a state a correct guest does not reach. It inherits the same reachability blocker.

### `mapledmaadvance` (MED) -- filed 2026-09-10, split out of `mapledmaaddr` so that round can proceed

`maple_do_dma_xfer()` accumulates `addr += datalen_cmd * 4;` across the command list and then, at its
tail, immediately before asserting the DMA-done event:

    // TODO: Should the DMA address be updated?
    d->dmaaddr = addr;

**The comment is the finding.** An advancing cursor is modelled, and the author recorded that they did not
know whether it should be. This is not a defect anyone has established -- it is an unresolved semantic
question sitting in shipped code with no test either way.

**Two early returns leave the function before that tail and belong to the same question:** the
`!d->enable` path and the `addr & 0x1f` alignment refusal both return without touching `d->dmaaddr`, so
after an aborted transfer the field holds the programmed address while after a completed one it holds the
advanced one. Any settled contract has to cover both.

Settling it needs real Maple hardware behaviour, and **no Dreamcast or Maple documentation is present** --
established by `ls _scratchpad/*.pdf`, not assumed. So it needs a source fetched first, on the
`vmesbcp2` / `21066_66a_hrm` / `ddi0406` precedent where a seat's citation was obtained and then verified
locally rather than trusted.

*** THIS MUST NOT BLOCK `mapledmaaddr`, AND THE EARLIER HOLD ON THAT ROUND WAS AIMED AT THE WRONG ARM. ***
That round deletes a terminating call in the register's READ arm, which is a pure reporter of this field.
It neither creates nor resolves the question above -- and the same unverified address is **already** handed
to the DMA engine on every transfer, whether or not a guest ever reads it back. The dependency runs the
other way: whatever is settled here becomes the expected value of that round's disclosed after-DMA row,
which is precisely why that row is written to pin the read arm's contract rather than to certify the
advanced value as correct.


### `ppcrldimimask` / `ppcrlwimiwidth` -- DESIGNED 2026-09-10, and the review found a SECOND defect plus THREE new rows

`regress/artifacts/ppcrldimimask/codex_repair_20260910.txt` (GPT-6 Astra at max, zero content flags,
13,496 bytes). It confirmed every premise about `rldimi`, **refuted my premise about `rlwimi`**, and
turned up three defects nobody had asked about.

**`rldimi` -- FOUR coordinated edits, and my sketch had one of them.** `sh` really is `-1` on exit for
every SH including zero, the rotate body really is a correct `ROTL64`, and the mask really does always
run to bit 63. But saving SH is not enough: the comparison happens *after* the increment, so the bound
is the endpoint's **successor**, and the counter must be **circular** because `MASK(MB, 63-SH)` wraps.

    int m, n = sh;                       /*  1: keep SH  */
    while (n-- != 0) { ... }             /*  2: consume the copy  */
    do {
            tmp |= ((uint64_t)1 << (63-m));
            m = (m + 1) & 63;            /*  3: circular increment  */
    } while (m != ((64 - sh) & 63));     /*  4: successor, modulo 64  */

**My description of the defect was half of it.** For non-wrapping masks the handler overwrites the low
SH bits that must survive; for **wrapping** masks it *omits* the required insertion into positions
`0..63-SH`, leaving those destination bits unchanged. A repair validated only on non-wrapping encodings
fixes one direction and leaves the other.

A partial repair that saves SH and fixes only the bound reaches `(uint64_t)1 << -1` at `MB=40, SH=40`.
**The seat declined to call that an infinite loop**, on the ground that doing so would assign defined
behaviour to an undefined program — which is the right discipline and is what my brief's question got
wrong.

**`rlwimi` -- a cast alone is NOT the repair.** The width contamination is confirmed as filed, but there
is a second defect at the same site: `ROTL32` is defined as rotating `x || x`, the low word **duplicated**,
and when `MB > ME` the mask wraps to cover every architectural position `0..31` — the whole high half. So
`RA`'s high 32 bits must be **replaced** with the rotated word, and this implementation preserves them
unconditionally.

**Scope: TWO rounds, not one.** One repairs operand lifetime and a circular inclusive traversal; the other
repairs source width and a missing high-word insertion, and validating it needs expectations outside the
doubleword detector's contract.

Both replacements were validated offline against an independent bit-membership oracle — 40,960 `rldimi`
cases and 655,360 `rlwimi` cases. **Neither was compiled**: the seat had no native compiler and WSL
returned `E_ACCESSDENIED`. This is a reading plus a model, not a measurement of this tree.

### `ppcwitnessmaskoracle` (MED) -- filed 2026-09-10. *** The oracle and the defect share the same misreading of the same sentence. ***

`regress/artifacts/ppcrldiclzero/opus_ppc_rldicl_witness_20260910.py` is a **committed** artifact of
`#522`. Two of its model oracles are wrong for wrapping masks, named by the review and then verified here
by opening the file:

* `want_rldimi()` computes the **intersection** of `bits mb..63` with `bits 0..63-sh`. Correct when
  `mb <= 63-sh`; when `mb > 63-sh` the two ranges are **disjoint and the intersection is empty**, so it
  returns the untouched destination for every wrapping encoding. Its own docstring shows how: it cites the
  manual's *prose* ("1 bits from bit MB through bit 63 - SH"), which is the non-wrapping reading, rather
  than the `MASK` definition that wraps.
* `mask32()` is documented "confined to the low 32 bits". Its companion `rotl32()` correctly returns the
  duplicated `(r32 << 32) | r32` — so the model *has* the duplication and then masks it away.

**This does not invalidate `#522`**, which is `rldicl` and uses neither oracle. The exposure is forward:
both sibling rows are filed on measurements this witness produced, and **the wrapping encodings are exactly
where both repairs do their new work**. An uncorrected oracle would score a correct repair wrong, or agree
with a repair that fixes only the non-wrapping half — a check that cannot fail, because the oracle omits
the wrap in the same way the implementation does.

### `ppcrlwhighhalf` (HIGH) -- filed 2026-09-10 as a dispute and RESOLVED THE SAME DAY as a DEFECT against Book I [L4 2026-10-09, 7n-3: this heading read "(MED) -- filed 2026-09-10, and it is a DISPUTE rather than a defect"]; rung-3 witness on committed HEAD: `regress/artifacts/ppcrlwhighhalf/witness_committed_20261009/`

I told the review that `rlwinm` and `rlwnm` are the correct idiom `rlwimi` fails to follow. **They are
correct about the low word and, on the RTL reading, wrong about the high one.** The decoder builds a
32-bit mask with a correct wrap; `X(rlwinm)` then holds `tmp` as `uint32_t` and assigns it into a 64-bit
register, which **zero-extends**, so the high half is unconditionally 0 where the RTL would put the
rotated word.

*** Filed as a dispute because the manual contradicts itself, and the seat said so rather than letting its
own reading stand unqualified: *** one line asserts blanket upper-half clearing for `rlwinm`, conflicting
with that instruction's RTL and with the general duplicated-rotation / wrapping-mask definitions. **This
row adopts neither reading.** Three further PowerPC manuals sit unconsulted in `_scratchpad/`, and
compiler expectations are the strong practical argument either way.

It must not block `ppcrlwimiwidth`'s narrowing half, which is wrong under every reading.

### `ppccr0modewidth` (MED; it said LOW until #554 re-graded it, 2026-10-02) -- filed 2026-09-10

`update_cr0()` branches on `cpu->cd.ppc.bits == 64` — the configured CPU **model** width, which never
changes while the guest runs — where the architecture selects the comparison width from the current
**mode** (the MSR SF bit, which can change at run time). On a 64-bit CPU executing in 32-bit mode, a result
whose low word is negative but whose full value is positive records GT where LT is required.

**Scope is the whole record form, not one instruction** — every `_dot` handler routes through this
function — which is why it is filed separately rather than inside either rotate row. LOW only because
reachability is unestablished in the sharpest possible way: it needs a 64-bit PowerPC CPU running with SF
clear, and no gate in this tree executes any 64-bit PowerPC instruction and checks the result. [2026-11-02, records: stale or too broad at 987cb596 -- the grade is MED since `#554`, as the heading says; gate 13 now runs 64-bit probes on the PPC970 (`regress/gate_ppc.sh:183` runs `ppc_rldicl_probe.py` on `-E bareppc`); and only the integer `_dot` handlers route through `update_cr0()` (the `DOT0`/`DOT1`/`DOT2` macros, `cpu_ppc_instr.c:208-213`), while the floating-point ones (`FDOT`, `:205-206`) update CR1 and `X(tlbsx_dot)` (`:3976`) writes CR0 itself]


### `mapledmaaddr` -- REVIEWED 2026-09-10: *** THE ROUND IS UNBLOCKED, AND MY DETECTOR WAS THE WEAK PART, NOT THE FIX ***

`regress/artifacts/mapledmaaddr/codex_readarm_20260910.txt` (GPT-6 Astra at max, zero content flags).
**Verdict: the read-arm correction may proceed independently of the cursor question.** The read arm
implements a separately testable rule -- *return the stored register field* -- while the cursor item
decides what the transfer routine should store there. The cursor policy already affects execution
regardless: a subsequent transfer starts from `d->dmaaddr`, so it already consumes the advanced value
whether or not any guest reads it.

**One claim of mine was too strong and the correction is exact.** "The edit does not change cursor
computation" is right; "the edit does not change the *observability* of that computation" would be
wrong -- a guest read that previously stopped execution can now obtain the field. The round must state
that as a new observable rather than call the diff behaviour-preserving.

**THREE CORRECTIONS TO WHAT I RECORDED EARLIER TODAY:**

1. The advance is **more than the payload term I quoted**: each descriptor advances by 8 bytes of
   control words + 4 bytes of command word + `4 * datalen_cmd` of data, so
   `C = (P + Σ(12 + 4*D_i)) mod 2^32`.
2. **"Advanced" does not mean numerically larger** -- the sum is modulo 2^32, and `C != P` is not
   guaranteed.
3. **My early-exit claim was wrong.** After an aborted transfer the field holds its **entry value**,
   which may be a *previous* transfer's cursor -- an early return preserves what was there rather than
   restoring a programmed address. The `!d->enable` test also precedes the alignment test, so a
   disabled *and* unaligned address never reaches the alignment diagnostic.

*** THE DETECTOR I PROPOSED IS INSUFFICIENT, and that is what changes the round. ***

* **Exact readback with no DMA is passed by four wrong implementations**: a constant equal to the one
  test value; constant zero against an initial-zero-only test; **alignment masking** against any test
  using only aligned values; and a snapshot of the last programmed address that never tracks DMA.
  Remedy: several distinct values including nonzero **high** bits and nonzero **low five** bits, with
  successive writes shown to replace what reads report.
* **Post-transfer inequality proves only that the answer differs from `P`** -- satisfied by zero, a
  fabricated `P + 4`, a stale cursor from an earlier transfer, or any masked transform. Independent DMA
  evidence rules out a *skipped* transfer; it says nothing about the value's relationship to the field.
* **The form that works**: capture the field value `S` immediately before the read; assert the delivered
  value equals `S` exactly, that the read leaves the field unchanged, and that the access returns
  normally with **no read-side diagnostic**.
* *** `MAPLE_STATE == 0` is not DMA evidence -- its read arm always returns zero, including after an
  early return. *** Use a supported command and verify a fresh expected response in a receive buffer
  pre-filled with distinguishable contents.
* **Keeping `fatal()` and deleting only `exit(1)` is rejected by no value assertion** if `fatal()`
  returns. Silence must be checked separately.


### `xscaleinten` -- REACHABILITY ANSWERED **YES** 2026-09-10, and my negative premise was false

`regress/artifacts/xscaleinten/codex_witness_20260910.txt`. This row now has a ratified disposition, a
confirmed guest path and a named test vehicle; it needs a measuring seat and nothing else.

**Two installers, both assigning before the `!machine->prom_emulation` early return** -- IQ80321 and
Iyonix. Selecting an XScale CPU is not enough: generic ARM init installs CP15 and CP14, never CP6. The
path is ordinary ARM dispatch with **no privilege or mode check anywhere in it**, and cold init already
selects SVC32 with interrupts masked.

*** I had guessed that nothing in `regress/` drives a coprocessor transfer. FIVE probes already execute
CP15 MRC/MCR on `cats`, *** and `footbridge_sites_probe.py` is the directly reusable pattern -- plant
instructions in RAM, set the pc, step, inspect registers -- pointed at IQ80321 instead. **No machine or
device addition is required**, which is what the witness ladder demands.

*[CORRECTED 2026-10-18 at the row's closure (the closure checks of GPT-6 Astra and Grok 4.7,
regress/artifacts/xscaleinten/close_20261018/, each finding it independently; verified at source): four of the five
run on `cats` (`footbridge_sites_probe.py`, `fbpending_witness.py`, `fbpending_drain_probe.py`,
`pit8253_latch_probe.py`); the fifth, gate 14's `arm_flags_probe.py`, runs on `testarm` -- as the ledger's copy of
this sentence says.]*

**An oracle trap that applies well beyond this row: a printed step disassembly does NOT prove the
instruction executed, or even that its condition passed** -- the engine prints the disassembly *before*
executing it. Any probe treating a stepped disassembly line as evidence of execution is asserting
something the engine does not promise.

A naive "write W, read, expect W" has four indistinguishable failures, including a read that never
executes -- which passes whenever the destination already holds W, and is especially easy if the
write-source register doubles as the read destination. The discriminating form uses two distinct
nonzero values, separate source and destination registers, and a destination pre-set to a third value,
plus **continuation and silence**: the current code already assigns the destination before terminating,
so the assignment alone is not the outcome under test.

**The same vehicle reaches every other termination in this function** -- interrupt steering, interrupt
acknowledge, and the shared `unknown:` label -- but *** each needs its own process invocation, because
the first `exit(1)` reached prevents observing any later one. *** That groups the coverage work without
implying the repairs should be identical.

A count in my brief was wrong: `crm=1` has **sixteen** direction arms, not fourteen. All sixteen are
locally quiet, but "quiet" does not mean "plain accessor" -- `tcr0` and `tcr1` increment before
returning their values, and a `tisr` write clears bits and deasserts timer interrupts. A sibling-parity
argument resting on "the timer arms are plain storage" would be wrong.


### `sgirandomcolour` -- *** `#519` DOES NOT CLOSE.  PASS 2 MEASURED A FLOOR BREACH, 2026-09-11. ***

*[CORRECTED 2026-10-18 by the 7n-5 ruling (`regress/artifacts/fablequeue7n_20261009/fable5_rule7n_35.md`; GPT-6 Astra confirming, and naming
this heading): the heading is HISTORICAL and its grade is wrong.  `#519` shipped as `fd15065` with the 89-row
instrument, after the 59 -> 77 -> 89 repairs -- not the 59-row one this entry calls shipped.  The six escapes below are
measured and real, but each is clause (e): the body tests `tile_nr` only at `>= 256` (tiled) and `>= 32` (LIN_A), `x`
and `y` only against their bounds (`< 0`, `>= 2048`), `*color` not at all, and the twelve nibbles that reach `default:`
only as that one cell (D1, 2026-09-25).  The repairs were L1 strengthening on a severity
warrant, so no further pass was owed; the row closed 2026-10-18 with its REGRESS held.]*

**Six mutants score 59/59 on the shipped instrument and every one writes uninitialised host stack into
guest memory.** `regress/artifacts/sgirandomcolour/pass2_20260911/` -- 13 builds, 11 instrument runs,
13 controls.

    M30_tilenrdecline   if (tile_nr == 0) ok = 0;       59/59   tile 1, 0x70630000
    M31_tilenrguard     if (ok || tile_nr)              59/59   tile 1, 0x6368696e  <- ASCII "chin"
    M32_tilenrxdecline  if (tile_nr_x == 0) ok = 0;     59/59   tile 1
    M33_tiledorigin     if (linear || y == 0) ok = 0;   59/59   tiled (0,1)
    M28r                the disclosed escape, replicated  59/59
    M37_fgvalue         if (*color == 0xaabbccdd)       59/59

**The smallest is eleven characters: `if (ok)` -> `if (ok || tile_nr)`.**

*** THE NEGATIVE CONTROLS ARE WHAT MAKE IT A FINDING. *** `|| ofs`, `|| x` and `|| y` each score
**58/59**, killed by exactly one row -- so the probe *does* see geometry. It cannot reach the tile
**index**: its only (4,1) cell is LINEAR, where `x >> 12 == 0`, and a tiled (4,1) would not have
helped either since `x / tilewidth == 0` at every bufdepth.

**Severity inverts the usual picture.** At 32bpp a tile is 128x128, so `tile_nr == 0` is
`x < 128 && y < 128`. On the default 1280x1024 framebuffer M30 **keeps the fix over 1.25% of the
screen and re-opens it over the other 98.75%** -- and all 59 rows sit inside the 1.25%.

*** THE CAUSE IS A WRONG WARRANT OF MINE THAT HAD ALREADY BEEN REUSED. *** The clause-(d) flow test
was applied **correctly** to `tlb_mode` -- floor axis, via `tileptr` -- and then **stopped at the
ARRAY and never reached the INDEX**. `tileptr = d->re_tlb_a[tile_nr] << 16`, so `tile_nr` reaches the
guarded store's address operand at least as directly as `tlb_mode` does, and `#100` in that same
function already calls `tile_nr` guest-derived and bounds it. My PRETABLE named only `tlb_mode` and
`bufdepth` as `ofs`'s dependencies, while `ofs = 512*y + (x % tilewidth) * bufdepth` contains x and y.

*[CORRECTED 2026-10-18 by the 7n-5 ruling: flow is not the test.  `tlb_mode` is a label the body tests as a case AND flows into
`tileptr`; `tile_nr` flows and is tested only at `>= 256` (tiled) and `>= 32` (LIN_A), never for zero, so the tile-index
family is clause (e).  Flow alone is the transitive chasing the 2026-08-24 DEPENDS-ON bound forbids.]*

**Three reading seats independently found the warrant false before the measurement showed what it
cost**, and one of them made the symmetry argument outright: `M13` (bufdepth), `M14` (linear) and
`M28` (color_mode) are **one guard-weakening shape on three fields**, so *"an instrument-relative
escape is not a contract-relative exemption."*

**This is the THIRD consecutive pass finding that shape, so the class-closure rule bites: the next
repair owes the closure in ONE diff, not another cell.** The 16-cell closure was principled and
**incomplete on its own principle**. Reachability is a `sw` to `DE_MODE_DST`, not a driver design
choice.

*[CORRECTED 2026-10-18 by the 7n-5 ruling: no closure was owed.  The cells were clause (e), so the closure that
followed (59 -> 77 -> 89 rows) was L1 strengthening chosen on a severity warrant.]*

**Also measured, and it trims rather than grows the instrument:** the four `ann cum` rows earn no kill
(delete them and `M5`/`M7` still die via `ann1`/`once`); `tA/tB/tC silent` kill sets are strict
subsets of the matching `ann1` sets; and `ycrcb x4y1` discriminated nothing until the pass-2 mutants
existed. **Rows that carry no kill are score noise.**

### `wdcdiagerr` (MED) -- the premise is INVERTED: `0x01` is the CORRECT code, and the defect is the coupling

ATA-2 `:2534` and `:5083`: a device completing diagnostics without error **sets the Error register to
`01h`**. So the value the model writes is right.

**The defect is that `d->error` is ONE variable serving TWO registers with opposite meanings** --
`dev_wdc.c:1843` [at 987cb596: `:1932-1934`, `case wd_error:` ... `odata = d->error;`] returns it as the **Error register**, and `:594` uses it to raise the **Status**
register's `ERR` flag inside `status_byte()`. The tree's own header shows the collision:
`WDCS_ERR = 0x01` and `WDCE_AMNF = 0x01`, the same number in different registers.

**So after EXECUTE DEVICE DIAGNOSTIC the model reports diagnostic SUCCESS in Error and command
FAILURE in Status, simultaneously** -- and `01h` is precisely the value that exposes the conflation. A
one-line change to the diagnostic value would leave `ERR` wrong.

### `wdcpktstatus` -- TWO ROUNDS, not one, and it needs a standard this tree does not have

My hypothesis that this and `wdcdiagerr` were one defect is **refuted on a zero: there are NO reads of
the ATAPI transfer's status anywhere in `dev_wdc.c`.** The backend's `res` is consumed and tested only
for `== 0` / `== 1`; the recorded status is never read and is freed at the next dispatch. So for a
dispatched packet on an existing image, **ERR has no implemented route to rise** -- `status_byte()`
returns `DRDY|DSC = 0x50` and Error stays `0x00`. Separating the storage repairs the diagnostic row
and leaves this one untouched.

*** AND ATA-2 DOES NOT SPECIFY ATAPI PACKET COMPLETION. *** It contains no ATAPI, PACKET or CHECK
CONDITION definition and explicitly **reserves `A0h-AFh`** (`:5828`) -- which is the model's own PACKET
opcode. **A claim about required ATAPI behaviour sourced from ATA-2 would be sourced from the wrong
standard.** Settling this needs the separate packet specification.

### `wdcaltownership` -- ATA-2 makes the two addresses SEPARABLE, which licenses the narrowing

`CS1-` is *"the chip select signal from the host used to select the Control Block Registers"*, and the
register address within that block comes from the three `DA` signals (`:1226-1234`). Selecting the
block and selecting an address inside it are **separate mechanisms**, so a device may answer one
control-block address and decline another.

**That makes `wdcaltdigin`'s narrowing disposition conformant at the ATA level, not merely
convenient.** ATA-2 does **not** arbitrate PC host-port ownership; that stays open.

### `wdccylwrap` (LOW -> MED) -- a clamp is the WRONG fix

ATA-2 `:2807`: word 1 is *"the number of user-addressable logical **cylinders** in the default
translation mode"* -- a **count**, not the highest address, with logical-to-physical mapping
vendor-specific. And Annex D `:5590`: *"For drives less than or equal to 528 MB, Identify Data word 1
shall not specify a value greater than 1,024."*

The witnessed case is a **32 MiB** image with heads = sectors = 1, giving 65,536 cylinders -- **a
breach of that limit by a factor of 64 before anything overflows.** The zero in word 1 is the symptom
of a bad geometry choice, not an independent arithmetic defect.

*** So clamping would replace a meaningless zero with a PLAUSIBLE WRONG NUMBER, which is strictly
worse -- a zero is visibly broken and a plausible count is not. *** The repair is to choose a default
translation geometry that fits sixteen bits and covers the image, and the CHS mapping must then use
it, since the transfer offsets read the same arrays.

**Annex D is INFORMATIVE** -- *"maximum compatibility is achieved if the following rules are obeyed"* --
and its *shall* does not change that. The fetched document is a **Revision 4c working draft** whose own
cover says it is not an approved standard.

### `ppcwitnessmaskoracle` -- both corrections VERIFIED against Book I; the PowerPC blocker is cleared

Endpoints, wrap direction, the `+32` offsets, the `& 63`, and both partition counts
(2016 + 2080 = 4096; 528 + 496 = 1024) all hold. **And the assertion is legitimate** -- I had made
*"It is not possible to specify an all-zero mask"* an `assert`, and an assert resting on a
non-normative sentence would fire on a legal encoding, which would be worse than the defect it
replaced. `ppcrldimimask` and `ppcrlwimiwidth` can now be measured without the oracle being the thing
that is wrong.

### `mipsextsignext` -- DROPPED, not a defect

The restriction is real and explicit (Restrictions block **and** Operation pseudocode, with
`NotWordValue` formally defined) -- but **UNPREDICTABLE says results MAY vary, and may-vary is not
must-vary**, so the model's truncation selects a *permitted* result where the architecture specifies
none. It also corrected my scope in both directions: the requirement **also** governs `INS`, for both
operands, and does **not** govern any doubleword form. A round that had generalised across the family
would have added checks to six instructions the architecture does not restrict.

### `m88kexcdetectorl2` (HIGH -> LOW) -- the sweep was neither a sweep nor a failure

The row's own title says M1/M2 delete `implemented = true;` at **DATA_ACCESS or RESET** -- vectors 3
and 0. **The probe drives neither**: `grep -c 'V_RESET|V_DATA|V_INTERRUPT|V_INSTR'` returns **0**, and
its 62 rows drive vectors 4-10, 114, the reserved 11/50/127 and the user traps. So the byte-identical
transcripts are the **correct and expected** result; the mutated code never executes.

Three parties reasoned about it without checking which vectors the probe drives -- the filer called it
a floor breach, I called it an apparatus failure, and a design review said the source predicts red
(true only for arms the probe drives). **The rule question held for the flagship seat is withdrawn:
the L2-versus-clause-(e) choice presupposed that a mutant in the detector's reach had escaped, and
none had.**

### `codexfarmclobber` (MED) -- a missing output file means "never started" ONLY for tools that create it at launch

`codexfarm.py` calls `subprocess.run()`, which BLOCKS for the whole call, and writes its answer file
only AFTERWARDS.  So for the entire run -- 6m41s in the measured case -- **there is no answer file at
all**, and the carrier's discriminator *log MISSING -> the command NEVER STARTED* reads that as dead.

That rule is correct for a SHELL REDIRECT, which creates the file before it execs, and exactly wrong
for a tool that writes at the end.  I applied it, concluded a job had never started, and re-fired codex
at the SAME output path with a `>` redirect -- which truncates at launch.  **A completed 12,032-byte
answer was destroyed by its own replacement.**

The cross-check that should have caught it is one this project has ALREADY recorded as blind here:
git-bash `ps -ef` prints the executable path and no arguments, so `grep -c -i codex` returns 0 whether
or not anything is running.  **Two apparatus checks, both blind, both failing in the same direction** --
and the one signal that WAS available went unconsulted: the harness tracks background jobs and notifies
on exit, so *"has it finished?"* was answerable without touching the filesystem.

FIXED STRUCTURALLY, because *remember that codexfarm writes late* is exactly the prose this project
has measured does not fire: a `<out>.RUNNING` sentinel written BEFORE the call and removed after the
answer lands, so mid-run and never-started stop rendering the same; plus a REFUSAL to launch when a
live sentinel or a NON-EMPTY answer already exists at the target path.  Negative-controlled in both
directions -- a non-empty answer refuses and survives intact at its original byte count, a live sentinel
refuses and names the owning pid, a CLEAN path is NOT refused, and `CODEXFARM_FORCE=1` overrides both.

OPEN because the tool lives in the session scratchpad rather than in `GXEMUL-SEC/tools/`, so nothing is
owed to the repo for the fix itself.  **What is owed is the carrier-level correction**: the discriminator
is stated there without its qualifier, and it is wrong for every tool in this project that writes its
output at the end rather than streaming it -- `agy` being the other one already on record.

### `landiskintc` (MED) -- six guest accesses per boot to UNMAPPED SH7751R extended-INTC registers

OpenBSD 7.6 on landisk touches **`0xfe080000` five times per boot** (`intc_init`) and **`0xfe080040` once** (`intpri_intr_priority`).  Both are SH7751R extended-INTC registers and **neither is claimed by any device in the constructed machine**, so all six accesses reach nothing.

**What is NOT established is the severity question itself:** whether the guest's interrupt-priority configuration is thereby wrong, or whether these writes are redundant with the base INTC registers the model does implement.  A write that lands nowhere and a write that lands nowhere AND MATTERS are different defects; the census counts accesses, not consequences.

First step: `dev_sh4.c`'s INTC handling against `_scratchpad/sh7750_hardware.txt`.  **The SH manual is present** -- this project once treated "there is no SH documentation" as load-bearing for four rounds, and it was false.

Measured in `regress/artifacts/landiskaux/census_20260827/RESULTS.txt`, whose write-up corrected itself to name all five unmapped sites per boot.  Filed 2026-09-11 because that correction had been made and then recorded in no row.

### `landiskboardreg` (MED) -- eight guest accesses per boot to UNMAPPED landisk board registers, including the RTC chip-enable

`0x10000003` is touched **five times per boot from `rtc_ce`** -- the RTC chip-enable -- and `0x10000005` **three times** from `intr_init` / `extintr_establish`.  Neither is claimed by any device in the constructed machine.

**The RTC half is a testable prediction rather than a guess.**  The machine DOES construct an `rs5c313` RTC at `0x110000000`.  If `rtc_ce` is the chip-select the guest drives to reach it, then the RTC conversation is happening with its select line going nowhere -- which either works by accident, because the model ignores chip-select, or does not work at all.  **Check which before assigning severity; the two outcomes differ by a lot and both are informative.**

`0x10000003` also appears in the `wdcstandby` row.  **That may be an unrelated coincidence of a common constant** -- it has NOT been established that they share a subject, and a round should check rather than assume.

Measured in the same census.  Filed 2026-09-11.

### `agentmodelwall` (MED) -- a MODEL wall on the Agent tool is not a TRANSPORT outage

**Measured 2026-09-11, during a real double outage.**  Opus 5 hit a session limit (`resets 6:10am`, HTTP 429) and killed **four in-flight subagents at once**; Fable 5 was already walled on its own quota, tested three times that day.  Both are Anthropic seats behind the **same Agent-tool transport**, and both are compile-and-measure front ends -- the roster weakness the carrier records from `#462`.

*** But the transport was never down.  Two subagents launched on `model: sonnet` started normally in the same minute. ***

**A MODEL WALL AND A TRANSPORT OUTAGE PRESENT IDENTICALLY** -- an Agent call that fails -- **and they have different remedies.**  `#462`'s outage was `API Error: 529 Overloaded` on the path, and nothing could be done but wait.  A per-model rate limit leaves the path healthy and the other models on it reachable.

**The discriminator is in the error text and costs nothing to read:** a `529 Overloaded` names no model and is the transport; a `429 rate_limit` naming `model sent to the API: claude-opus-5` is that model only.

**Recoverable and not recoverable are different here.**  READING capacity is fully recoverable -- a sonnet subagent has the same repo tools and can do records audits, source tracing and harvests.  **MEASURING capacity is not equivalent**: the carrier's claim for Opus is that it is *the seat most likely to compile and measure*, which is a statement about judgement rather than permission.  Whether a sonnet measurement carries the same weight is **not established** and must not be assumed -- substituting it silently and reporting the result as the flagship's is the seat-failure-counted-as-agreement shape wearing a model name.

**Operational rule:** when an Agent call fails, read WHICH MODEL the error names before concluding the transport is gone, and try another model on the same path.  One invocation settles it -- exactly as the wall rule already says for CLI seats.

Filed because the cost was real: for about ten minutes subagent capacity was treated as lost while it was available the whole time.  Same shape as the kimi substitute sitting unfired for days.

### `pit8253flood` (MED) -- filed 2026-09-16 from `#530`'s closing pass 5, found while measuring something else

**`dev_8253.c` has TWO GUEST-DRIVABLE `fatal()` ARMS WITH NO LATCH, and a previous round of this project put them
there.**  An ordinary 16-bit MSB write to counter 1 or counter 2 reaches:

```c
	case 1:	fatal("TODO: DMA refresh?\n");
		break;	/*  #223: (Codex/Fable) warn+ignore, don't exit() the host  */
	case 2:	fatal("TODO: 8253 tone generation?\n");
		break;
```

**`#223` did the de-fatalisation and did not bound what it left behind.**  Both arms used to end the process; both now
announce, unconditionally, once per write.  `grep -cE 'static int|warned|\(once\)' src/devices/dev_8253.c` returns
**ZERO** -- the file carries no latch of any kind.

**MEASURED, not estimated:** the `#530` c5 measuring seat's 150-row 8253 prototype counts the emissions and prints the
count -- **18 of each per session, 36 per run**.  It moves no row (the probe parses `print` output), which is why it is
a filed item and not a `#530` finding.

*** THIS IS THE CARRIER'S OWN STANDING RULE UNMET, AT A SITE THIS PROJECT CREATED. ***  *"A guest-drivable `fatal()`
needs a latch and not a verbosity flag"* -- and the reason is measured elsewhere in the tree: `fatal()` has **no
early-out at all** (`src/core/debugmsg.c`, the `fatal()` body against `debug()`'s `if ((quiet_mode && !ss) || v < 0)
return;`), so `-q` cannot silence it.  The house idiom is **N = 1 per DEVICE INSTANCE plus an explicit `(once)`
marker**, which is ~82% of all suppression markers in `src/devices/`.

It is also the DE-ESCALATION CLAUSE seen from the other side: `#223` removed a host kill -- correctly -- and with it
the accidental tripwire that made the path self-announcing exactly once, leaving an unbounded announce that nothing
counts.

**WHAT IT OWES WHEN TAKEN** (it is NOT owed by any shipped round, and `#530` deliberately did not ride it along):
* the rung-3 ATTEMPT the lifecycle ruling requires -- and most of a witness already exists, since the c5 seat's
  prototype reaches both arms from an ordinary guest store on an unmodified machine;
* the per-instance latch in the `(once)` idiom;
* an ACCEPT row proving the legal MSB write still lands.  *** THE WARRANT GIVEN HERE WAS WRONG AND IS
  CORRECTED IN PLACE (L4, 2026-09-17, Fable 5.1 adjudication; codex raised it independently). ***  This
  bullet used to read *"the de-escalation clause applies, because the fix removes nothing but the flood"*.
  **That REVERSES the clause's own premise.**  The clause binds a fix that REMOVES A HOST-FATAL GUARD,
  because doing so destroys the accidental tripwire that made guard growth self-announcing.  `#223` removed
  every kill in this file four rounds ago and the live `exit()` count is ZERO, so this round removes no such
  guard and **the de-escalation clause is INAPPLICABLE** -- stated explicitly rather than left blank, because
  an unrun check and an inapplicable one must not render the same.
  **BUT CLAUSE (d) IS APPLICABLE AND THIS ENTRY NEVER MENTIONED IT:** the fix ADDS predicates where the code
  had none (`if (!d->warned_x)` at each latched site), so under DEPENDS-ON each owes a null-repair mutant.
  The smallest is ONE WORD -- `d->warned_tone` to `static int warned_tone` -- and every emission-count row
  stays GREEN under it, because a single-machine probe has one device instance.  That shape is live in the
  tree (`dev_pcc2.c:486`, `dev_osiop.c`, `dev_dec21143.c`), so a copy-paste reproduces it by accident; the
  recommended kill is a SOURCE-LEVEL PRESENCE ROW asserting no `static int` occurs in this file.  Behavioural
  accept rows still have value on ordinary regression grounds -- a count-only detector would miss a latch
  guard accidentally enclosing the servicing code -- but that is a separate justification, not an invocation
  of the host-kill clause;
* **a sibling census, not an assumption:** the neighbouring `default: fatal("[ 8253: huh? writing to counter %i but
  neither from msb nor lsb? ]")` is the same shape and must be counted, not guessed at.  Related rows: `floodclass`,
  `staticlatchscope`.

*One caution for whoever takes it, from the same seat's reading: an MSB write to counter **0** takes a different path
(`timer_add` / `timer_update_frequency` with `hz = 1193182/counter`), so a row that programs a SMALL counter installs a
high-frequency host timer.  Keep the programmed counter large.*

*** PASS 1 RAN 2026-09-17 (panel_20260917_063557, NINE seats, PANEL_COMPLETE, no seat failure).
THE PANEL CHANGED THIS ROUND SUBSTANTIALLY AND THE SCOPE IS NOW FIVE SITES, NOT SEVEN. ***

* **`:351`/`:354` ARE DEAD CODE.**  `DEV_8253_LENGTH` is 4 and there is ONE registration tree-wide, so
  `relative_addr` is in {0,1,2,3} exactly; `I8253_TIMER_CNTR0/1/2` are 0/1/2 and `I8253_TIMER_MODE` is
  3, so all four values have named cases and the outer `default:` can never fire.  Three packet-fed
  seats correctly refused to settle this and each named the missing fact -- the registered mapping
  length, which the brief failed to inline.  Latching them would be the addition licence's

`DEVICE_ACCESS(macepci)`, 530 LINES DOWN THE SAME FILE -- and the sibling is WORSE, because it does
not decline at all.**  Verified by reading, not taken from the seat:

```c
 722| DEVICE_ACCESS(macepci)
 ...
 728| 	if (len != 4)
 729| 		fatal("[ macepci: unimplemented len %i ]\n", len);
 730|
 731| 	if (writeflag == MEM_WRITE) {
 732| 		idata = memory_readmax64(cpu, data, len);
```

There is **no `goto`, no `return` and no latch**.  A narrow access prints -- unlatched, so it FLOODS --
and then **falls through into the switch with the wrong length anyway**, which is precisely the
behaviour `#529`'s comment enumerates as the reason its own `goto` exists.

*** AND IT CORRECTS A RECORDS DEFECT IN THIS FILE, which I made worse before I made it better. ***
The straddling-access entry above cites this site in a list of *"register-width devices that REJECT an
unexpected length"*.  **`macepci` does not reject.**  The citation was ALSO stale (`:698`, moved to
`:728` by `#529`'s own diff), and correcting only the NUMBER left the false CLAIM standing -- *a
correction is not safer than the thing it corrects*.  Both halves are now fixed.

**SEVERITY, stated honestly:** MED rather than HIGH.  No witness exists yet -- whether a guest driver
issues a narrow access to macepci config space is UNKNOWN, and the `#529` witness does not transfer
(it was at CRIME).  **A round taking this owes the rung-3 ATTEMPT first**, per the 2026-08-27 ruling.
The option set is the six-membered one; the tree's own answer for this exact shape is `#529`'s --
DECLINE + LATCHED ANNOUNCE with `(once)` in the text.

### `crimectlflood` (LOW-MED) -- filed 2026-09-17, same provenance.  **IT HAS A DETECTOR COST, AND
### THAT IS THE WHOLE REASON TO FILE IT RATHER THAN JUST FIX IT.**

`dev_sgi_ip32.c:377-379` is a guest-drivable UNLATCHED `fatal()` -- every CONTROL write carrying a
bit the model does not implement prints, with no `(once)` marker and no latch:

```c
 375| 			idata &= ~CRIME_CONTROL_ENDIANESS;
 376|
 377| 			if (idata != 0)
 378| 				fatal("[ CRIME_CONTROL: unimplemented "
 379| 				    "control 0x%016llx ]\n", (long long)idata);
```

It is the same class as `pit8253flood` and belongs to `floodclass`.

> *** BUT LATCHING IT WOULD RED A SHIPPED DETECTOR ROW, AND THE COUPLING IS EXACT. ***
> `regress/crime_width_probe.py:1612` (as first committed, 7440e129; the :1256 / 3 form was the uncommitted probe of 2026-09-18) is
> `row("p acc ctl msg", count(t, "CRIME_CONTROL: unimplemented", clean), 4, ...)` -- it COUNTS this
> very message and expects **4**, one per accepted CONTROL write (`0x01` sd, `0x0001` sw, `0x0201` sw, `0x0201` sd) [corrected 2026-11-02, records: said `:1256`, 3 and three writes].
> A latch takes that count to **1** and reds the row.

**So this is not a free tidy-up.**  Whoever takes it must re-pin that row IN THE ORACLE-CORRECTION
ORDER -- re-pin first, measure the committed build RED under the new expectation, THEN change the
